reverse_outline.summary: Key points: two leaders drew the same organization differently with nothing to say which was right; a leader's work is joining decisions; decisions are joined in four places
Corvane's new CPO and its CTO each drew the organization and disagreed about who led eleven teams
Such disputes are usually settled around people or by template, and both views skip the question of what each role is for, so the two drawings could not be compared on merit

Part V's claim that leadership structure is derived from the decisions that must be joined (executive roles, triad, spans and layers, technical track); roadmap of this page and of the four chapters and their questions

A leader's distinctive work is joining decisions that teams would otherwise make separately; because earlier parts already show which decisions fall between teams and functions, the structure can be derived from them

Joining costs scarce judgment and adds delay and distance, so every role and layer must pass a test: it joins decisions the units below cannot; the test maps onto the book's two lenses, system design and product thinking

results.draft_locus: Four Places Where Decisions Are Joined ¶1 (item 'At the top')
results.quote: The common configurations are a CTO and a CPO as peers, one executive who holds both, and a CTO with a VP Engineering. Each trades one kind of joining for another: two peers keep what is built and how it is built in balance and join them slowly, by negotiation, and one executive joins them fast, in one head, and leans to one side.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated (a): three configurations are named and 'Each trades...' promises a trade for each, but only two are explained; 'a CTO with a VP Engineering' is left without its trade and without saying where product sits, and both readers supplied the assumption that the chapter covers it. Wording within the item; the spec's order is fine.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 7 (first reported by flow reader A, item 1)
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, decision 'waive by rule' under the rule 'max two rounds per chapter': this finding remained after the last check round allowed. It was listed in the writer's report to the author; where the writer revised the unit afterwards, the revision was not re-checked by fresh readers, and where the writer left the unit unchanged, the finding stands as written.

results.quote: The test corresponds to the two lenses through which this book looks at organizations, system design and product thinking.
results.finding: Reader B (a, item 6) did not know why the lenses are raised here, between the test and its application, and assumed they come from earlier in the book; reader A (b, item 4) found the turn unannounced and 'corresponds' unexplained but resolved it within the paragraph. Both note that the last sentence adds a measure (how long the teams wait) that is not the test as stated, and both suggest moving the lenses next to 'Every chapter carries both lenses'. Not blocking because A rated (b). The spec places the lenses in p05, so a move is the author's decision; a clause saying why they are named here is a draft change.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶3 against Four Places ¶1 (item 'Down the line')
results.quote: the levels of management between the executives and the teams, follow from team size.
results.finding: Reader B (a, item 3) went back to the opening: here layers follow from team size, in the list 'The number of layers follows by arithmetic from headcount and those spans', and B stayed unsure what happens to the arithmetic when a layer fails the test ('a layer is kept only if it passes the test'). Reader A (b, item 8) noticed the same mismatch and resolved it from the bullet. Not blocking because A rated (b).

results.draft_locus: Four Places Where Decisions Are Joined ¶2
results.quote: Spans and layers come third because they say how many levels there are; start with them, and the layers are counted before anyone knows what the top layer is.
results.finding: Reader A only (a, item 2): after 'repeated at each level below', the reason for spans and layers reads like a reason to put them before the triad, since the number of levels is not yet known; A supplied the assumption that the triad's repetition does not depend on the count. Both readers (A item 2, B item 9, rated b by B) first read 'start with them' as an instruction and not as 'if one started with them'. The ordering point is one reader's, so it is not corroborated.

results.draft_locus: Four Places Where Decisions Are Joined ¶2

results.quote: The two drawings disagreed about who led eleven of the teams.
results.finding: Reader B only (a, item 1): the page never says how the drawings differed; B assumed each leader had put the eleven teams under themselves and read on. The spec's hook and p01 give only this, and the spec's open questions leave the detail to chapter 18, so the gap is the spec's.

results.quote: So the leadership structure can be derived from that architecture.
results.finding: Both flow readers, both rated (b) (A item 5, B item 5): 'that architecture' has not been used as a name on the page; each re-read the previous sentence to take it as the team boundaries, product model and engineering model together. Not blocking.

results.quote: A team decides with its own information; it cannot make its decisions together with another team's, another function's, or next year's.
results.finding: Both flow readers, both rated (b) (A item 6, B item 4): 'or next year's' breaks the pattern of the list (next year's what?); resolved on re-reading and by the next sentence. Not blocking.

results.finding: Opens on a concrete scenario and the question it leaves open; no dictionary definition, apology, announcement-only or sweeping-generality opening.

The closing synthesizes (top down and then across teams), reads the Corvane drawings against the lead's question and hands off; it does not merely restate, apologize or raise an unrelated new point. It does not spend the part's closing verdict (a declared non-goal).

Synthesis ('the four chapters build a leadership structure from the top down and then across teams') and so-what ('a leader can explain each role and each layer by the decisions it joins, and can remove or decline one that joins none') are both present, with the takeaway (open the chapter that answers your question; otherwise read in order) and the hand-off to executive-roles-and-reporting-lines.

'At Corvane the CTO and the CPO argued about who should lead the eleven teams, and nobody had asked what each role was for, which is why both drawings could be defended and neither could be shown to be right' reads the opening drawings against the lead's question, as the spec's callback states.

The cold intro reader predicted both roadmap promises in order: what a leader is for (joining decisions, the delay each role must earn), then the four places in the declared order, closing on four chapters answering four questions with a return to Corvane. Its extra guesses (a table, a return to the drawings inside the first section) are not roadmap promises.

The cold reader named the four subjects in reading order with their slugs: executive roles and reporting lines; the product-engineering-design triad; spans, layers and managers of managers; staff-plus and architects. This matches the criterion's expected answer.
